prompt.context: You are a scientist. You have just invented the world's first everlasting light bulb. Fortunately, you have been granted a rock-solid patent for it. The current light bulb industry is a global monopoly.
prompt.question: How much is the patent worth?

clarifying_info.q: How long does the patent last?

clarifying_info.a: You are valuing the patent, not an individual everlasting light bulb.

clarifying_info.q: Does the bulb have commercial applications (offices, cars, etc.)?
clarifying_info.a: This is a domestic light bulb only — no commercial applications such as offices or cars.

clarifying_info.q: What is the global population and how many people have electricity?
clarifying_info.a: There are 6 billion people in the world. Assume only 4 billion have access to electricity.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average household size?
clarifying_info.a: Assume 8 people per household on average.

clarifying_info.q: What do conventional and everlasting bulbs cost?
clarifying_info.a: Conventional light bulbs price: $2. Everlasting light bulbs will be priced at $5.

clarifying_info.q: How long do conventional bulbs last?
Will consumers switch to the everlasting bulb?
clarifying_info.a: Assume everyone switches to everlasting in year one.
Assume a 20% profit margin on both conventional and everlasting bulbs.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use?

framework: Size the current conventional light bulb market (revenue and profit)
Determine whether consumers would switch to the everlasting bulb and why
Size the one-time revenue and profit opportunity from the everlasting bulb
Establish the standalone value of the patent to the scientist (without monopoly infrastructure)
Analyze the negotiation dynamics: who is the buyer, what is each party's walk-away value
Arrive at a defensible patent valuation accounting for the scientist's cost to commercialize

questions.prompt: Size the current conventional light bulb market — what is the annual profit to the existing monopoly?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up from population: 4B people with electricity / 8 people per HH = 500M households. Assume 5 rooms per HH = 2.5B rooms. Assume 2 bulbs per room = 5B domestic bulbs globally. At $2 per bulb but bulbs last 2 years, annual sales = 5B / 2 = 2.5B bulbs/year, revenue = $5B/year. At 20% margin, annual profit = $1B/year. A common error is to forget that bulbs last 2 years and quote $10B/year revenue.

math.setup: 4B people / 8 per HH = 500M HH; 500M HH * 5 rooms * 2 bulbs = 5B bulbs installed; bulbs last 2 years so annual replacement = 2.5B bulbs; revenue = 2.5B * $2 = $5B/year; profit = $5B * 20% = $1B/year
steps: 5B bulbs / 2 year lifespan = 2,500,000,000 replacement bulbs per year
math.answer: $1B per year in profit for the conventional monopoly

questions.prompt: Would consumers switch from conventional ($2, lasts 2 years) to the everlasting bulb ($5, lasts forever)?
questions.guidance: Yes — $2 every 2 years means the consumer spends $1/year on average per bulb. The everlasting bulb costs $5 once. It pays for itself in 5 years and is free thereafter. This is an obvious value proposition for the consumer. Candidate should articulate the payback period clearly.

math.setup: Compare annualized cost: conventional = $2 / 2 years = $1/year; everlasting = $5 one-time; payback = $5 / $1/year
steps: Conventional annualized cost per bulb: $2 / 2 years = $1/year
After year 5, everlasting costs $0 per year vs. $1/year for conventional
math.answer: Consumers would switch; payback is 5 years and the everlasting bulb is strictly cheaper long-term

questions.prompt: What is the one-time revenue and profit from selling the everlasting bulb to the entire global domestic market?
questions.guidance: There are 5B domestic bulbs installed. Everyone buys exactly one everlasting bulb. Revenue = 5B * $5 = $25B one-time. A key trap is to treat this as annual revenue — it is a one-time event because the bulb lasts forever. Profit = $25B * 20% = $5B one-time.

math.setup: 5B installed bulbs * $5 per everlasting bulb = $25B one-time revenue; profit = $25B * 20%
math.answer: $5B one-time profit — NOT a recurring annual figure

questions.prompt: The monopoly currently earns $1B/year in profit. At a 5% discount rate in perpetuity, is the patent worth $20B?
questions.guidance: This is the first conceptual trap. The interviewer may suggest $1B/year / 5% = $20B. The candidate should push back: the everlasting bulb DESTROYS the conventional industry — the monopoly loses its $1B/year stream entirely once everyone switches. The patent is not worth the NPV of the stream it replaces; that stream goes to zero. The candidate should resist anchoring on the monopoly's current profit.

math.setup: NPV of $1B perpetuity at 5%: $1B / 0.05 = $20B — but this stream disappears once everlasting bulbs displace conventional
steps: However, the conventional market ceases to exist after the switch — this $20B NPV is destroyed, not captured
math.answer: $20B is a trap; the conventional profit stream is eliminated, not preserved

questions.prompt: The monopoly is the only potential buyer. What is the maximum the monopoly would rationally pay for the patent?
questions.guidance: The monopoly should pay less than $5B (the standalone value of the patent to the scientist). If the scientist sells for anything up to $5B, the monopoly is better off than letting a competitor exploit the patent. But since the monopoly is the sole buyer (bulletproof patent, domestic market monopoly), they have pricing power. The minimum the scientist would accept is any amount above $0 (or above their commercialization cost). Rational floor for the monopoly's offer: $5B and one cent — just enough to make it worth the scientist's while, keeping the surplus for the monopoly.

math.setup: Scientist's standalone value = $5B one-time profit (at 20% margin, no infrastructure cost assumed). Monopoly avoids $5B loss by buying. Rational maximum monopoly pays = just above $5B to beat the scientist going independent; rational minimum = just above scientist's reservation price.
steps: Scientist's value if independent: $5B one-time profit (with 20% margin)
Monopoly's value of blocking: preserves existing $1B/year stream ($20B NPV) AND captures the $5B one-time market — total value of ownership is substantial
But external buyer (non-monopoly) would only pay up to $5B standalone
Monopoly as sole buyer need only pay $5B + $0.01 to acquire
math.answer: Monopoly pays $5B and one cent — just above the scientist's standalone value

questions.prompt: The scientist has no sales and marketing infrastructure. Assuming $500M in sales costs, what is the patent actually worth?
questions.guidance: The scientist's real net value from going independent is not $5B but $5B minus the cost of building a distribution/sales infrastructure. If that cost is $500M, the standalone value drops to $4.5B. Therefore the monopoly can acquire for $4.5B and one cent. The candidate should confidently land here and defend it. The 'right' answer to the case is $4.5B and one cent.

math.setup: Scientist net profit = $5B gross profit - $500M commercialization cost = $4.5B; monopoly floor bid = $4.5B + $0.01
math.answer: Patent is worth $4.5B and one cent

recommendation: The patent is worth approximately $4.5B — specifically $4.5B and one cent, representing the scientist's net standalone value ($5B one-time profit minus $500M commercialization costs)
The monopoly, as the sole rational buyer, needs to pay only marginally above this floor; any higher price transfers surplus unnecessarily to the scientist
risks: The scientist could find a way to commercialize without full infrastructure (e.g., licensing to retailers), raising their reservation price
Third-party buyers could emerge if the patent covers only the technology, not the market monopoly, allowing competition
Regulatory intervention could limit the monopoly's ability to suppress the technology
Discount rate and cost estimates are sensitive assumptions; $4.5B could shift materially
next_steps: Verify the patent's scope and defensibility against workarounds
Assess realistic commercialization cost estimates beyond the $500M assumption
Model sensitivity of the valuation to discount rate and margin assumptions
Consider whether the monopoly has a legal obligation to license the patent under antitrust law
